bibliographic.title: The Switch, the Ladder, and the Matrix: Models for Classifying AI Systems
bibliographic.authors: Jakob Mökander, Margi Sheth, David S. Watson, Luciano Floridi
bibliographic.citation_apa: Mökander, J., Sheth, M., Watson, D. S., & Floridi, L. (2023). The Switch, the Ladder, and the Matrix: Models for classifying AI systems. Minds and Machines, 33, 223–250. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-022-09620-y

methodology.study_design: Narrative review and comparison of prior AI system classification approaches organized into three mental models
methodology.technology_context: General artificial intelligence systems, including machine learning and hybrid approaches; governance illustrations reference EU AIA and other policy frameworks; no conversational AI or LLM focus in provided text

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article directly addresses AI governance material scope through a comparative review of classification models (Switch, Ladder, Matrix), which is relevant to governance framing in regulated settings. However, the provided text contains no focus on conversational systems, chatbots, agents, LLMs, RAG, guardrails, observability, or other operational conversational governance mechanisms central to the review scope.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Extracted metadata contains errors (year listed as 2019; publication_type listed as conference_paper) and only partial full text was supplied; confirm study selection, methodology section, and absence of conversational/LLM content in remaining pages.

appraisal.notes: Objective and conceptual contribution are clearly stated, with a structured three-model synthesis suited to governance demarcation. Appraisal of sampling, search strategy, data collection, limitations, and ethics reflexivity is limited because those details are not present in the supplied excerpts.

cerqual.explanation: The framework is conceptually coherent and clearly presented, but methodological details are unclear from the provided text and the article's direct relevance to conversational LLM governance is only partial.

coding.subtheme: Switch, Ladder, and Matrix classification models
rq_alignment: partial alignment to governance and regulated-context questions
low alignment to conversational AI and LLM-specific governance mechanisms

synthesis.main_claim: Organizations lack a well-defined material scope for operationalizing AI ethics, and prior attempts to classify AI systems for governance can be grouped into three mental models: the Switch (binary), the Ladder (risk-based), and the Matrix (multi-dimensional).
synthesis.contribution: Provides a conceptual vocabulary and comparative framework to help organizations design, deploy, or regulate AI systems by demarcating which systems fall within AI governance frameworks.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence for governance material scope, AI system classification, and risk-based regulatory framing; do not treat as central evidence on conversational or LLM-specific governance unless additional sections explicitly cover those topics.

evidence.claim: Study objective is to review and compare AI classification approaches for governance practice.

evidence.claim: Core contribution is three mental models for classifying AI systems.

evidence.claim: The Ladder is a risk-based classification model.
evidence.excerpt: the Ladder, i.e., a risk-based approach that classifies systems according to the ethical risks they pose

evidence.claim: The Matrix is a multi-dimensional classification model.
evidence.excerpt: the Matrix, i.e., a multi-dimensional classification of systems that take various aspects into account, such as context, input data, and decision-model
